claims.claim: Le Guin says she has often named events or places in her fantasies that she did not yet know anything about, which were merely words when she wrote them.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin', ursulakleguin.com, 2005
claims.quote: when I wrote them, merely words
claims.page: body, on the later exploits of Ged

claims.claim: Le Guin asserts that the more exact and factual the detail in a fantasy story, the more plausible the imagined world will be.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin', ursulakleguin.com, 2005
claims.quote: Exact and vivid words make an exact and vivid world.
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'Then there is detail'

claims.claim: Le Guin names coherence as the touchstone of plausibility in imaginative fiction.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Plausibility in Fantasy: an open letter to Alexei Mutovkin', ursulakleguin.com, 2005
claims.quote: The touchstone to plausibility in imaginative fiction is probably coherence.

claims.claim: Le Guin says what constitutes plausibility in fantasy is the coherence of the story and its consistent self-reference.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Plausibility Revisited', ursulakleguin.com, 2005
claims.quote: What constitutes plausibility in fantasy is the coherence of the story
claims.page: body, paragraph on fantasy's contract with the reader

claims.claim: Le Guin objects that a preindustrial fantasy setting is no justification for a world having no economics and no social justice.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Some Assumptions about Fantasy', speech at the Children's Literature Breakfast, BookExpo America, Chicago, 4 June 2004
claims.quote: no economics and no social justice

claims.claim: Le Guin says she feels like setting off fireworks whenever she finds a fantasy set in a genuinely imagined society and culture.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Some Assumptions about Fantasy', BookExpo America, 4 June 2004
claims.quote: genuinely imagined society and culture instead of this lazy-minded

claims.claim: Le Guin defines a society's technology as how it copes with physical reality, and lists food, clothing, power sources, what people build with and what they build, and their medicine.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'A Rant About "Technology"', ursulakleguin.com, 2005
claims.quote: how people get and keep and cook food
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'Its technology is how a society copes'

claims.claim: Le Guin defines technology as the active human interface with the material world.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'A Rant About "Technology"', ursulakleguin.com, 2005
claims.quote: Technology is the active human interface with the material world.

claims.claim: Le Guin says that thanks to 'show don't tell' she finds writers in her workshops who are afraid to describe the world they have invented.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy', first published in the Los Angeles Times, 5 January 2003, as 'When to Bend, When to Break'
claims.quote: They’re afraid to describe the world they’ve invented.

claims.claim: Le Guin argues the narrator's voice, disparaged as omniscient, is the most intimate voice of all rather than a distancing one.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy', Los Angeles Times, 5 January 2003
claims.quote: it’s the most intimate voice of all

claims.claim: Le Guin says the same fear of distancing leads writers to abandon the narrative past tense for the tight-focused present tense, and answers that distance lends enchantment.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy', Los Angeles Times, 5 January 2003

claims.claim: Le Guin says writing is made of words that are bodily, and that the rhythms of words are bodily rhythms.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'What Makes a Story', ursulakleguin.com, c. 2007
claims.quote: the rhythms of words are bodily rhythms

claims.claim: Le Guin says many contemporary writers avoid complex sentences and write what she calls Macho Staccato.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Joe', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 part 3', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.quote: avoid complex sentences and write what I call Macho Staccato

claims.claim: Le Guin says the ideal is flexibility, a balance of different sentence lengths depending on what the sentences do.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Michael', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 part 3', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.quote: The ideal is flexibility, a balance of different sentence lengths

claims.claim: Le Guin says a poet's desire to make words vivid, exact and as few as possible carries over into writing prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Deepthi', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 part 3', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.quote: as exact and accurate, and as few as possible

verdicts.trueWording: “in my fantasies, I have often mentioned events or places which I didn’t yet know anything about … These were, when I wrote them, merely words — ‘empty’ nouns.”
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched live (HTTP 200), tags stripped. Quote exact. Page says 'mentioned' where the claim says 'named'; the page's own gloss '“empty” nouns' plus the named example (the later exploits of Ged in A Wizard of Earthsea) supports 'named'. Page locator confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: “The more realistic, exact, ‘factual’ detail in a fantasy story … the more plausible the world will be. … Exact and vivid words make an exact and vivid world.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact, and it is the sentence immediately following the claim sentence in the same paragraph beginning 'Then there is detail' — locator confirmed. Both limbs (exact/factual detail; greater plausibility) on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: “The touchstone to plausibility in imaginative fiction is probably coherence.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact, in the paragraph before the closing two — locator confirmed. One nuance recorded, not a downgrade: Le Guin hedges with 'probably', which the claim drops; no limb of the claim is otherwise unsupported. The page continues 'Fantasy, which creates a world, must be strictly coherent to its own terms.'

verdicts.trueWording: “What constitutes plausibility in fantasy is the coherence of the story, its consistent self-reference.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact and both limbs (coherence; consistent self-reference) are the one sentence, in the paragraph on fantasy's 'contract with the reader' — locator confirmed. Essay dated 2005 on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: “It may resemble mediaeval Europe in being preindustrial — but that doesn’t justify its having no economics and no social justice.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact, inside Assumption 2 ('Fantasy Land is the Middle Ages') — locator confirmed. Speech header on the page confirms Children’s Literature Breakfast, BookExpo America, Chicago, 4 June 2004.

verdicts.trueWording: “Whenever I find a fantasy that is set in a genuinely imagined society and culture … I feel like setting off fireworks.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact (page continues 'recycled hokum'), in Assumption 2 — locator confirmed. Both limbs (genuinely imagined society and culture; fireworks) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “Its technology is how a society copes with physical reality: how people get and keep and cook food, how they clothe themselves, what their power sources are … what they build with and what they build, their medicine.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Every listed item in the claim — food, clothing, power sources, what they build with and what they build, medicine — appears in that one sentence, in the paragraph the locator names.

verdicts.trueWording: “Technology is the active human interface with the material world.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact and it does stand as its own one-sentence paragraph, as the locator says. Essay dated 2005 on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: “Thanks to ‘show don’t tell,’ I find writers in my workshops who think exposition is wicked. They’re afraid to describe the world they’ve invented.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact (curly apostrophes match). The claim compresses two consecutive sentences; both are on the page. It is the third body paragraph, as the locator says. Page footer confirms first publication as 'When to Bend, When to Break', Los Angeles Times, 05 January 2003.

verdicts.trueWording: “the narrator’s voice (ponderously described as ‘omniscient’) distances the story — whereas it’s the most intimate voice of all”
verdicts.note: Quote exact. The 'disparaged as omniscient' limb is carried by the page's 'ponderously described as “omniscient”'; the 'rather than a distancing one' limb by the page's 'whereas'. Fourth body paragraph — locator confirmed. Note the belief is attributed to the writers Le Guin is arguing against, which is how the claim reads it.

verdicts.trueWording: “The same fear of ‘distancing’ leads writers to abandon the narrative past tense … for the tight-focused, inflexible present tense. But distance lends enchantment…”
verdicts.note: Quote exact; every limb (same fear of distancing; abandoning narrative past tense; tight-focused present tense; distance lends enchantment) is in those two consecutive sentences of the fourth paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: “writing … is made of words, and words are bodily … and the rhythms of words are bodily rhythms.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact, in the paragraph beginning 'I use bodily similes not mechanical ones' — locator confirmed. Both limbs (words are bodily; rhythms of words are bodily rhythms) in one sentence. Page dated c. 2007.

verdicts.trueWording: “Many contemporary writers avoid complex sentences and write what I call Macho Staccato.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact and it opens Le Guin's answer to the questioner named Joe — attribution confirmed on the page. Page header: originally posted at Book View Café, 7 September 2015.

verdicts.trueWording: “The ideal is flexibility, a balance of different sentence lengths, longer and shorter sentences depending on what they do, what they’re about.”
verdicts.note: Quote exact, in the answer to Michael — attribution confirmed. The claim's 'depending on what the sentences do' limb is the page's 'depending on what they do, what they’re about'.

verdicts.trueWording: “the poet’s desire to make the words vivid, as exact and accurate, and as few as possible, telling much briefly”
verdicts.note: Quote exact. 'Carries over into writing prose' is supported by the preceding sentence ('the poet’s ear … will carry over into writing prose') and the elliptical 'And so may the poet’s desire…'. Two nuances recorded, neither a downgrade: Le Guin hedges with 'may', and the answer is a single joint reply under the heading 'POETRY AND FICTION — Two questions' to Joseph and Deepthi, not to Deepthi alone.
